content:
A decade after 52 per cent of Britons voted to leave the European Union, the British public has decisively turned against Brexit — but that does not mean voters want the government to rush back in. A cluster of new polls published this week paints a picture that is more complicated than either side of the debate would like: regret is now the majority view, yet rejoining the EU is still not the public's top priority.

The headline numbers, from [YouGov polling published on November 18](https://yougov.com/en-gb/articles/55982-public-opinion-on-a-rejoin-referendum), are stark. Fifty-eight per cent of Britons now say Britain was wrong to vote to leave the EU in 2016, against 32 per cent who say it was right. Sixty-three per cent describe Brexit as more of a failure than a success; only 9 per cent call it a success. The figures have pointed the same way for years — the share regretting Brexit has been higher than the share defending it since June 2021 — but the gap has rarely looked this wide.

That is the easy part. The harder question is what voters want done about it, and here the same polling tells a different story. Only 37 per cent of Britons think attempting to rejoin the EU should be a priority for the government, while 45 per cent say it should not be. Even among those who voted Remain in 2016, almost three in ten say rejoining should not be a priority right now. At the same time, 54 per cent say holding another referendum on EU membership within the next five years would be acceptable, against 33 per cent who disagree. The public, in other words, has largely made up its mind about the past but not about the timetable for the future — a gap the main parties will have to navigate carefully.

The political arithmetic, however, is starting to look tempting for Labour. According to GB Omnibus polling commissioned by Fortius Global and released earlier this week, support for Labour would jump by more than seven points if the party's next manifesto included a plan to rejoin the EU. Labour would reach 31.5 per cent among the total electorate on that promise, against 24.3 per cent in the baseline voting-intention question, in a poll of 7,291 voters. It is the kind of finding that helps explain why Prime Minister Andy Burnham has begun talking openly about putting Rejoin into Labour's next manifesto, a decade after the referendum he campaigned against.

Constituency-level polling points the same way. A YouGov survey commissioned by Best for Britain, based on an MRP analysis of all 632 parliamentary constituencies in Great Britain, found in September that restoring EU membership was the most popular approach to the bloc in every constituency bar four — Ashfield, Clacton, Great Yarmouth and Boston and Skegness, where "don't know" was the most common answer. Across 11,927 voters, 35 per cent named EU membership as their preferred government proposal, against 18 per cent who backed a closer relationship within the government's red lines and 11 per cent who wanted looser ties.

The regional picture reinforces the trend. In London, YouGov polling commissioned by mayor Lord Sadiq Khan found almost two-thirds of Londoners support rejoining the EU — 63 per cent — while 68 per cent favour rejoining the single market and/or customs union, and nearly half believe Brexit has made them worse off. In Northern Ireland, a LucidTalk survey for Queen's University Belfast found 63 per cent believe Brexit has caused far more disruption than they anticipated in 2016, 52 per cent agree the UK ought to rejoin under standard member obligations, and 77 per cent see a clear need for a "serious dialogue" about the long-term relationship. Support for the Windsor Framework, meanwhile, has fallen to 45 per cent, its lowest rating since June 2021.

The shift is not only about voters. British businesses overwhelmingly back rejoining, according to a major consultation by the UK Trade and Business Commission, which found three-quarters of firms saying restoring EU membership would have the most positive impact on their business. Researchers at the Centre for European Reform have calculated that exports of chemicals and pharmaceuticals are down 21 per cent since the UK left the EU, and agrifood exports down 29 per cent. A study by the Productivity Institute, reported by the Financial Times on Friday, goes further: rejoining the EU would add £112 billion a year to the British economy, more than twice the £54 billion a Swiss-style halfway house would deliver — a sum equivalent to the entire annual budget of the Department for Education — with investment flooding back if full membership were restored.

Even Leave voters are showing signs of buyer's remorse, though of a particular kind. A Savanta poll of 2,195 Britons, conducted ahead of Friday's EU-UK summit, found nearly half of Leave voters now want stronger cooperation with the EU on immigration — 48 per cent chose it as a priority, ahead of trade at 36 per cent and defence at 37 per cent. Reform UK voters were even clearer, with 50 per cent choosing migration cooperation. Among the public as a whole, cutting trade barriers was the top priority at 44 per cent, ahead of migration cooperation at 37 per cent and closer defence ties at 35 per cent. The European Council on Foreign Relations found 66 per cent of voters saying Brexit has had a negative impact on the cost of living, 65 per cent on the economy overall, 57 per cent on opportunities for young people, and 58 per cent even on controlling illegal immigration — one of the central arguments of the Leave campaign.

The debate is now being fought in the open again. Campaigners on both sides relaunched this weekend: Lord Michael Gove is leading the Stay Out campaign, while Get In! is positioned to lead the Rejoin campaign, The Independent reported on Saturday. Burnham himself, fresh from Friday's EU-UK summit in Brussels, has tried to hold two positions at once. The deal he signed — covering food and agriculture exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme that could open the door for 100,000 young Europeans to work temporarily in the UK — will add up to £17 billion a year to the British economy, he said, calling Friday "a good day for Britain and a good day for Europe". But he also described the package as "probably the limit" of what can be achieved before the next general election, and recommitted to Labour's manifesto red lines ruling out a return to the single market, the customs union or free movement.

The next year would be spent 'brainstorming' ideas with the EU for the future relationship, he said, adding that he hoped the UK would return to the EU in his lifetime. "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it," Burnham said after the summit. "But we want to inform the parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."

For now, the polls suggest the public is with him on the diagnosis but not yet on the prescription. A majority thinks Brexit was a mistake, a majority would accept another referendum within five years, and the electoral maths of promising rejoin looks strikingly favourable. But with the economy and immigration still ranked as voters' most important issues, and fewer than four in ten wanting rejoining made a priority, the route back to Europe — if it comes — is likely to be argued over manifesto by manifesto, not decided in a single leap. As [Le Monde noted in its analysis of the reopened debate](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2026/11/20/in-the-uk-andy-burnham-rekindles-brexit-debate-five-years-after-its-implementation_6785011_4.html), the more Burnham talks about it, the less clear the path seems — and that ambiguity may itself be the strategy.

For context on the deal Burnham signed on Friday, see our coverage of the [EU-UK reset agreement on food, carbon and youth mobility](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/eu-uk-reset-deal-food-carbon-youth-mobility-november-2026), and on the EU's wider spending plans, [the bloc's record €7.9 billion disbursement to Ukraine](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/eu-disburses-record-7-9-billion-ukraine-november-2026).
summary: A decade after the referendum, 58% of Britons say leaving the EU was wrong and 63% call Brexit a failure — yet only 37% want rejoining made a government priority, new YouGov and constituency polling shows, as Prime Minister Andy Burnham weighs putting Rejoin in Labour's next manifesto.
title: Polls show Britain has decisively turned against Brexit — but rejoining the EU is not yet a priority
